examTraps.theFix: Don't just match words—match the STORY! If 4 sentences are about 'new RBI rules for gold loans' and Sentence D says 'Gold jewelry is popular at Indian weddings', Sentence D is the Odd Intruder!
examTraps.examPattern: The Odd Sentence always shares 1-2 keywords with the passage to trick hasty readers.

practiceDrills.badge: Magnet Trick: 'This / These' Trail
practiceDrills.prompt: Find the mandatory pair among these 3 sentences: (A) Consequently, small exporters struggled to hedge their currency risk. (B) Exchange rates swung wildly after the sudden tariff announcement. (C) This volatility forced banks to widen their forex margins.
practiceDrills.whatSentenceSays: (B) introduces wild swings in exchange rates; (C) calls those wild swings 'This volatility'; (A) states the final consequence.
practiceDrills.whyTwoFeelCorrect: Both B and C talk about currency swings and volatility, so you know they belong together, but it's easy to get confused about whether B comes first or C comes first!
practiceDrills.howToPickWinner: Use Rule #1 on top (The 'This / These' Magnet Rule)! Sentence (C) starts with 'THIS volatility'. Ask: What volatility? You cannot say 'This volatility' until you first describe something swinging wildly! Sentence (B) says 'Exchange rates swung wildly'. So (B) MUST come first, and (C) ('This volatility...') snaps right behind it: BC!
practiceDrills.ruleRef: Refers to: Rule #1 (The 'This / These' Magnet Rule)

title: Column Matching
tagline: Check the Split-Point Glue & Only Test Pairs Given in the Options!
summary: Column 1 has 3 beginnings (A, B, C) and Column 2 has 3 endings (D, E, F). Never waste time testing all 9 possible combinations! Look at the 5 answer choices, pick one pair (like A–E), and check if the split-point fits both grammar and story!

plainDictionary.simpleMeaning: The exact spot where the last word of Column 1 touches the first word of Column 2. Read just 2 words before the split and 2 words after the split!
plainDictionary.examples: Col 1 ends in '...aimed at reducing' + Col 2 starts with 'credit risks' ➔ 'reducing credit risks' (Fits!).

decisionSteps.step: Step 1: Look at the 5 Options FIRST!
decisionSteps.action: See which pair appears in the options (e.g., A–D, B–E). Don't check pairs that aren't even in the options!
decisionSteps.outcome: Cuts your work in half immediately!

decisionSteps.step: Step 2: Do the 4-Word Split-Point Check
decisionSteps.action: Read the last 2 words of Column 1 + the first 2 words of Column 2.
decisionSteps.outcome: If Column 1 ends in 'to', Column 2 MUST start with a plain action word (or a thing). If it doesn't, that pair is dead!

decisionSteps.step: Step 3: Do the Topic Check
decisionSteps.action: Make sure Column 1 and Column 2 are talking about the same topic (don't join 'farming loans' with 'airline tickets'!).
decisionSteps.outcome: Catches traps where the grammar fits but the story is nonsense!

goldenRules.name: Rule #1: The 4-Word Split-Point Grammar Lock
goldenRules.formula:
Col 1 ends in 'TO' ➔ Col 2 starts with plain action word (verify, curb, improve)
Col 1 ends in 'OF / IN / FOR / BY / WITH' ➔ Col 2 starts with a Thing (noun) or '-ing' word
Col 1 ends in 'HAS / HAVE / HAD' ➔ Col 2 starts with 'been' or finished action word (-ed)
goldenRules.explanation: Before reading the whole sentence, just look at the last word of Column 1! It tells you what kind of word Column 2 MUST start with!
goldenRules.correctExample: ✅ Col 1: '...steps taken to' + Col 2: 'curb inflation in food prices.' ('to' + 'curb' = Match!)
goldenRules.incorrectExample: ❌ Col 1: '...steps taken to' + Col 2: 'curbing inflation...' ('to curbing' here is wrong!).
goldenRules.trick: Check the glue at the seam before reading the whole sentence!

examTraps.trapName: Trap #1: Grammar Fits, But Story Is Mixed Up!
examTraps.whyIntuitionFails: Col 1 ends in 'to improve' and Col 2 starts with 'weather forecasting', so the grammar sounds smooth—even though Col 1 was talking about 'ATM security'!
examTraps.theFix: After the 4-word grammar check passes, read the full combined sentence once to make sure the story makes sense!
examTraps.examPattern: Examiners always include 1 pair where the grammar fits at the seam, but the two topics don't match.

practiceDrills.badge: Split-Point Trick: Grammar + Story Check
practiceDrills.prompt: Column 1 (A): 'The new cyber-security rules require all payment apps to...' Which Column 2 ending fits (A)? (D) '...storing customer card data on foreign servers.' (E) '...encrypt sensitive customer PINs before transmission.' (F) '...monsoon rainfall across agricultural districts.'
practiceDrills.whatSentenceSays: Column 1 (A) is about cyber-security rules for payment apps and ends with the tiny word 'to'.
practiceDrills.whyTwoFeelCorrect: Both (D) and (E) talk about customer card data / PINs, which matches the cyber-security topic! So 'Both A–D and A–E' looks very tempting!
practiceDrills.howToPickWinner: Use Rule #1 on top (The 4-Word Split-Point Grammar Lock)! Column 1 (A) ends with 'require all payment apps TO'. After 'require [someone] to', we MUST have a plain action word (like 'encrypt'), NEVER an '-ing' word ('storing')! 'To storing' (A–D) is broken grammar! Only 'to encrypt' (A–E) passes both the grammar check and the story check!
practiceDrills.ruleRef: Refers to: Rule #1 (The 4-Word Split-Point Grammar Lock: require X to + plain action word)

title: Contextual Synonyms & Antonyms
tagline: Check 'Same vs Opposite' Direction & Watch for Secret Second Meanings
summary: The #1 reason students lose marks here is NOT difficult words—it is picking the SAME meaning (Synonym) when the question asked for the OPPOSITE meaning (Antonym), or forgetting that simple words like 'qualify' and 'reserve' have special office meanings!

plainDictionary.simpleMeaning: Synonym = Means the SAME thing (Good ➔ Good). Antonym = Means the OPPOSITE thing (Good ➔ Bad).

decisionSteps.step: Step 1: Look at the Question Instructions FIRST: Did it ask for SIMILAR or OPPOSITE?
decisionSteps.action: If it asks for OPPOSITE (Antonym), mentally shout 'OPPOSITE!' so you don't click Option A (which is almost always the same-meaning trap!).
decisionSteps.outcome: Saves you from the #1 careless mistake in exams!

decisionSteps.step: Step 2: Plug your choice back into the sentence
decisionSteps.action: For Synonym: When you swap the bold word with your answer, the sentence story must stay 100% the same.
decisionSteps.outcome: Catches words that look similar in a dictionary but don't fit a banking sentence!

goldenRules.name: Rule #1: Simple Words with Secret Bank/Office Meanings
goldenRules.formula:
QUALIFY a statement = Put a limit or warning on it (NOT pass an exam!)
DISINTERESTED judge/auditor = Fair, neutral, unbiased (NOT bored!)
CREDULOUS investor = Too gullible, believes fake tricks easily (NOT trustworthy!)
CREDITABLE performance = Worthy of praise, good (NOT gullible!)
EQUIVOCAL reply = Vague, unclear, hiding the truth on purpose
goldenRules.explanation: When an exam asks for the meaning of an easy-looking word like 'qualify' in a sentence, it is NEVER testing the childhood meaning ('pass a test')—it is testing how the sentence uses it ('limit or soften a claim')!
goldenRules.correctExample: ✅ 'The spokesperson QUALIFIED her promise by noting it depended on tax collections.' (Here 'qualified' = limited / made conditional!)
goldenRules.incorrectExample: ❌ Picking 'passed' or 'certified' for 'qualified' in that sentence.
goldenRules.trick: Never answer without reading the sentence! Pretend the bold word is a blank and see what word the sentence needs!

examTraps.trapName: Trap #1: Option A in an Antonym Question Is Always the Synonym!
examTraps.whyIntuitionFails: Your eyes see the bold word 'EXPLICIT' (clear), and Option A says 'Clear / Obvious'. Your brain goes 'Hey, explicit means clear!' and clicks Option A—forgetting the question asked for the OPPOSITE!
examTraps.theFix: Before looking at options A, B, C, D, E, check if the question says 'MOST SIMILAR' or 'MOST OPPOSITE'!
examTraps.examPattern: In every Antonym question, Option A is a trap Synonym.

practiceDrills.badge: Secret Meaning Trick: What Does 'Qualified' Mean Here?
practiceDrills.prompt: In the sentence: 'While the rating agency praised the bank's loan growth, it QUALIFIED its outlook by pointing to rising unsecured defaults' — which word is NEAREST in meaning to QUALIFIED?
practiceDrills.whatSentenceSays: The agency praised the bank (+), BUT added a warning/limit (-) by pointing to rising bad loans.
practiceDrills.whyTwoFeelCorrect: Outside this sentence, everyone knows 'qualified' means 'certified / passed an exam'! So 'certified' feels immediately familiar!
practiceDrills.howToPickWinner: Use Rule #1 on top (Simple Words with Secret Bank Meanings)! Put 'certified' into the sentence: '...certified its outlook by pointing to rising defaults.' Does pointing to bad defaults 'certify' an outlook? No! Pointing to bad defaults LIMITS or PUTS A WARNING on the positive outlook! So 'moderated / restricted' is the exact winner!
practiceDrills.ruleRef: Refers to: Rule #1 (QUALIFY a statement = put a limit/warning on it)

title: Spelling & Confusable Words
tagline: Easy Letter Tricks for Twin Words (Principal/Principle, Stationery/Stationary)
summary: Two words that sound identical (like 'principal' and 'principle' or 'compliment' and 'complement') are super easy to tell apart once you know the 1-Letter Secret inside each word!

plainDictionary.simpleMeaning: Two words that sound the exact same when spoken out loud, but have a 1-letter difference in spelling that completely changes the meaning!
plainDictionary.examples: Principal vs Principle | Stationery vs Stationary | Compliment vs Complement

decisionSteps.step: Step 1: Use the 1-Letter Memory Trick (Rule #1 below)
decisionSteps.action: Look at the single letter that changes between the two twin words (like E vs A, or I vs E, or LE vs PAL).
decisionSteps.outcome: Matches the right twin with 100% certainty!

decisionSteps.step: Step 2: Count Double Letters in Long Words
decisionSteps.action: Check 'accommodate' (2 C's + 2 M's), 'embarrass' (2 R's + 2 S's), 'occurrence' (2 C's + 2 R's).
decisionSteps.outcome: Spots spelling traps immediately!

goldenRules.name: Rule #1: The 1-Letter Memory Tricks for the Top 6 Confusable Twins
goldenRules.formula:
1. Princi-PLE (ends in LE like ru-LE) = A moral rule or law
   Princi-PAL (ends in PAL) = Main person (school head) OR Main loan money ('principal amount')
2. Station-E-ry (has E for Envelope) = Paper, pens, envelopes
   Station-A-ry (has A for Anchor) = Standing still, not moving
3. Compl-I-ment (has I = 'I look nice!') = Praise / nice words
   Compl-E-ment (has E = compl-E-te) = Something that completes or goes well with another thing
4. DIS-interested = Fair, neutral, taking no side (like a good referee)
   UN-interested = Bored, yawning, doesn't care
5. DIS-creet (two E's together peering quietly) = Careful, quiet, keeping secrets safe
   DIS-crete (T separates the E's!) = Separate, distinct pieces
6. AD-verse = Harmful / bad ('adverse impact')
   A-verse (no D!) = Strongly disliking ('averse to risk')
goldenRules.explanation: Never guess between these twins! Just look at the secret letter inside the word!
goldenRules.correctExample:
✅ The borrower repaid the PRINCIPAL (main loan money) with interest.
✅ Mobile banking COMPLEMENTS (completes/enhances) branch banking.
goldenRules.incorrectExample: ❌ The borrower repaid the PRINCIPLE amount. (Wrong twin—'le' is for moral rules!)
goldenRules.trick: LE = ruLE | PAL = main money/person | E = Envelope OR complEte | A = Anchor (still) | I = 'I look nice' (praise)!

examTraps.whyIntuitionFails: Students think 'Principal' is only the headmaster of a school, so for banking they pick 'Principle'!
examTraps.theFix: In banking, 'principal' means the 'MAIN / FIRST' money lent (before interest). So loan money is ALWAYS 'princi-PAL' (never '-ple')!
examTraps.examPattern: 'principal sum / principal repayment' = ALWAYS ends in -PAL!

practiceDrills.badge: Confusable Twins: Complement vs Compliment
practiceDrills.prompt: The bank's new doorstep service is designed to ___ its rural digital kiosks rather than replace them.
practiceDrills.whatSentenceSays: The doorstep service works alongside and completes the digital kiosks (making them better together) instead of replacing them.
practiceDrills.whyTwoFeelCorrect: 'Compliment' (with an I) and 'complement' (with an E) sound 100% identical when you read them in your head!
practiceDrills.howToPickWinner: Use Rule #1 on top (The 1-Letter Memory Trick)! Ask: Is the doorstep service telling the kiosk 'Ooh, you look pretty today!' (Praise = Compl-I-ment with an I)? Or is it COMPLETING and pairing well with the kiosk (Compl-E-ment with an E, like compl-E-te)? It is completing/enhancing it—so pick 'complement' (with an E)!
practiceDrills.ruleRef: Refers to: Rule #1 (Compl-E-ment = complEtes vs Compl-I-ment = praise)

title: Advanced Mixed & Hybrid Practice
tagline: Solve One Easy Piece First to Eliminate 3 Options in Multi-Part Questions
summary: Advanced questions combine two jobs at once (like filling a blank AND fixing a grammar error). Don't panic! Solve the easier job first—that kills 3 wrong options in 5 seconds, leaving you only 2 choices to compare!

plainDictionary.simpleMeaning: A question that asks you to do two things at the same time (e.g., pick a connector AND spot a grammar mistake). If an option gets Part 1 wrong, you don't even need to check Part 2!
plainDictionary.examples: Eliminate by the easiest part first!

decisionSteps.step: Step 1: Solve the Fastest Check First (Tiny Glue Word or Action Word Check)
decisionSteps.action: Look for a quick lock like 'Although vs Despite', 'comply WITH vs adhere TO', or 'One vs Many (was vs were)'.
decisionSteps.outcome: Cross out all options that fail that simple rule!

decisionSteps.step: Step 2: Compare Only the 2 Surviving Options
decisionSteps.action: Look at the ONE spot where Option A and Option B differ.
decisionSteps.outcome: Pick the winner without wasting time reading all 5 options from scratch!

goldenRules.name: Rule #1: The 'Divide and Conquer' Trick
goldenRules.formula: Check Lock #1 (Connector / Preposition) ➔ Kill 3 options ➔ Compare the 2 survivors on Lock #2 (Grammar)
goldenRules.explanation: A long 3-line question is just two tiny easy questions glued together! Never judge the whole 3-line sentence at once. Check your Connector Rule first, then check your One-vs-Many Grammar Rule second!
goldenRules.correctExample: ✅ Step 1: Blank has 'was' after it ➔ must be 'Although' (kills 3 'Despite' options). Step 2: 'Each of the banks' needs 'has' (kills the 'have' option). Done!
goldenRules.incorrectExample: ❌ Re-reading the entire 3-line sentence 5 times.
goldenRules.trick: Use the exact same rules from Connectors, Grammar, and Cloze—one step at a time!

examTraps.trapName: Trap #1: Getting Scared by Long Sentences
examTraps.whyIntuitionFails: When a sentence has 35 words, students think the rule must be super complicated.
examTraps.theFix: The longer the sentence in a bank exam, the SIMPLER the actual grammar mistake hiding inside it (usually just 'was vs were', 'despite vs although', or 'than vs than that of')!

practiceDrills.badge: Two-in-One Trick: Connector + Grammar Lock
practiceDrills.prompt: Choose the pair that correctly completes the sentence: '___ the new payment gateway was faster, each of the partner banks ___ required to run a seven-day safety trial.'
practiceDrills.whatSentenceSays: Part 1: Even though the gateway was faster (Surprise!); Part 2: Each bank was still required to run a safety test.
practiceDrills.whyTwoFeelCorrect: Once you spot 'Although' for Blank 1, both 'Although ... was' and 'Although ... were' look close because 'partner banks' is plural right before Blank 2!
practiceDrills.howToPickWinner: Use Rule #1 (Divide & Conquer)! Lock 1 (Blank 1): After Blank 1 we have 'the new payment gateway WAS faster' (has action word 'WAS'). That kills 'Despite' and 'Because of'! Only Options B and C survive! Lock 2 (Blank 2): 'EACH of the partner banks ___'. Remember our Grammar Rule: 'Each of' is ALWAYS ONE (Singular)! So 'were' dies, and 'Although ... was' wins 100%!
practiceDrills.ruleRef: Refers to: Connector Rule #1 (Action Word Check) + Grammar Rule #2 ('Each of' = Singular)
